lede.tech: **{Works} live works** where medicine, the military and frontier AI meet, built by a **medical student** and **military officer** with AI as the engineering tool. **{lines} lines** across {files} files in {systems} of them. Every one is live, and this page asks each address to answer while you read.
lede.plain: {Works} working projects, built by one person in spare time. I'm a **medical student** and **military officer**, and AI wrote most of the code with me. **Everything here is live**, and this page checks that for you the moment it loads.

purpose.tech: This site documents {months} months of learning and building in spare hours. These projects were made possible by tools that lowered the technical barrier between an idea and working software. Others will bring different experience and build better things.
purpose.plain: This site documents {months} months of learning and building {works} working projects in spare time. New tools made it easier to turn ideas into software. Other people will bring different experience and build better things.

scope.tech: Everything listed is deployed and public. The site does not take that on faith: when a page loads, your browser asks every address to answer, and records what came back beside its name. The front page sets out the work by world, then the writing and the films. This page is the change record for the site itself.
scope.plain: Everything here is online and public. When a page loads, it checks each app from your own browser and shows the result beside its name. The front page has the apps, then the writing and the videos. This page explains why the site keeps getting rebuilt.

method.tech: Every system was specified by the author and written with Claude, then verified the way a clinician verifies a lab: against a source, by a second reader, and against the live deployment rather than the local copy. Medical content carries its citations. Scoring tables cite the governing publication. Where a source deck was wrong, the question was corrected and the correction logged.
method.plain: I describe what I want, the AI writes it, and then it gets checked the way a doctor checks a test result: against a trusted source, by a second reviewer, and on the real live site. Medical facts show where they came from.

note.tech: Study tools on this site are for exam preparation and are not medical advice. Clinical calculators and field references are teaching aids; confirm with the governing guideline before use on a patient.
note.plain: The study tools here are for exam practice and are not medical advice. The calculators and references are teaching aids: check the official guideline before using one on a patient.

caution.tech: The probe is an opaque cross-origin fetch, so it can only report that a host answered, not that the answer was the right page. Treat a filled dot as "the lights are on", and click through for anything that matters.
caution.plain: The check only proves that each site answered, not that the page it sent back was the right one. A filled dot means the lights are on. Click through for anything that matters.

practice.tech: This site is rebuilt from the ground up at every new Anthropic model class, as a personal benchmark of frontier capability. Each edition is designed end to end by the model it is named for, then **retired, not deleted**, when its successor arrives. The archive is the measurement: put two volumes side by side and you can see, in typography and judgment rather than benchmark scores, how far the frontier moved. Vol. 01 wore the newsroom, Vol. 02 wore the clinic, and Vol. 03 wore the uniform, then four more costumes at once. Vol. 04 wears nothing: it sets each work beside its own earlier edition and lets you look.
practice.plain: Every time a new class of Claude comes out, I have it redesign this entire site. The old version gets retired and archived, not deleted. Compare any two editions side by side and you can see how much better the models are getting: **taste is harder to fake than a test score**. This edition does the comparing for you.

since.tech: What changed since Vol. 03 was issued in September, beyond the design. The five views are retired together and the site is one edition again, built from one record, so a count can no longer disagree with itself between pages. Great Books, AdmissionsAcademy, the music, Monitoring the Situation and Force Multipliers joined the work, and the Lab opened in October. {Kept} apps now have an earlier edition kept at its own address, most of them redesigned from a blank page by Claude Opus 5.5 in September. Every description was checked again on 9 November 2026 against the source and the live app, and corrected where the app had moved on or the claim was more than the record supports. The lines were recounted from source: {lines} in {files} files, up from {previous_lines} in {previous_files}. Two things this edition adds that no earlier volume had: the work itself, shown as it looks today, and each earlier edition set beside it.
since.plain: Since the last edition: the five switchable designs were retired and the site is one design again. A medicine course was added, along with a tracker of what the internet is talking about, a set of how-to cards and a music page. Most of the apps were redesigned, and their old versions are still online. Every description was checked again against the real app. This edition also shows you a picture of every app, and can put the old version next to the new one.

text.lab_rules: Every lesson opens with what you will be able to do and how long it takes, ends with a quiz and a one-page summary, and has a Clinical values tab: typical adult reference ranges from standard textbooks and guidelines, each one cited, drawn against the lesson as it runs. Educational only and not for clinical use; no drug doses. Your progress stays in this browser: no accounts, no trackers, and it works on a phone and with a keyboard.
text.lab_review: Ten questions drawn from the lessons you have started, shuffled together, each with its answer explained and a link back to the step that teaches it. Mixing topics is harder than one lesson's quiz, which is what makes it stick.

text.notes_rules: Every post has the same shape: one lead story, a few notes from other desks, and one read on the day. Each claim links to the story or the post it rests on, and every figure is printed beside its source. A post that breaks a rule is not built.

Built by a chunk, author, review, adversarial-triage pipeline that caught and corrected about 100 factual errors in the commercial source decks during authoring and 90 more in triage.
works.plain: Free practice questions and study guides for the Step 2 CK and COMLEX subjects: nearly 13,000 questions, every one checked against its source card and most read again by an independent reviewer, plus a test mode that works like the commercial question banks.

works.name: Patient Handoff Tracker

Flask and SQLite on a free tier, so the first load wakes the server.
works.plain: A digital checklist for doctors handing off patients between shifts, a step the Joint Commission names as a leading cause of serious safety events. Built as an emergency medicine quality improvement project, with made-up patients only. The first load can take 30 to 60 seconds while the free server wakes up.
works.kw: medicine ipass sbar emergency department flask quality improvement

works.name: Read This
works.tech: Pattern-interpretation trainer: 28 procedurally generated rhythm strips at 25 mm/s with calipers and a live monitor, a fixed 8-step read of 14 twelve-lead cases with MI localization by territory, and an outside-in chest film read over synthesized radiographs and real films. Every case sourced.
works.plain: Learn to read heart tracings and chest X-rays the same disciplined way every time. Draws realistic EKGs from medical criteria, then quizzes you.
works.kw: medicine ekg ecg rhythms 12-lead cardiology chest x-ray

works.name: MICRO TD
works.tech: Tower defense where the body is the map: 16 guideline cases as levels, 34 real drugs as towers against 25 organisms, damage set by coverage and site penetration, resistance bred by antibiotic pressure, and organ toxicity, plus a one-patient Ward Rounds mode. TypeScript and Canvas, every fact sourced, 104 tests.
works.plain: Treat infections as a tower defense game: every tower is a real antibiotic that only works where it reaches and against the germs it covers. Broad drugs breed resistance, and every drug costs the patient something. Built to make studying infectious disease feel like a game.
works.kw: medicine game tower defense antibiotics microbiology typescript

works.name: Anatomy Bench
works.tech: The human body as 1,659 separately named structures in eleven layers, built from the open BodyParts3D atlas and keyed to the Foundational Model of Anatomy. A builder simplifies, quantizes and packs 2.3 million triangles into 14 MB; the page draws them in WebGL2 with no library, one mesh a layer, each structure's state held in a texture. Layers go solid, ghost or off; any structure can be named, peeled, isolated or cut by a section plane; two quiz drills. A bench: each model that works on it leaves a dated run.
works.plain: A body you can turn, take apart and cut through, one named structure at a time: bones, muscles, vessels, organs and brain. Click anything to learn its name and where it belongs, search for a structure, or have it quiz you. It names and places structures; it does not yet teach what they do. For study, not for patient care.
works.kw: medicine anatomy 3d body atlas skeleton muscles vessels brain webgl quiz bodyparts3d fma

papers.name: The Frontier AI Risk Stack
papers.tech: Frontier AI risk is best understood not as a single category but as a stack of six interacting layers. The most serious dangers arise from the way failures compound across layers: a structured analytical tool for policymakers, developers, and civil society.
papers.plain: AI risk isn't one problem, it's six problems stacked on top of each other, and the biggest dangers come from these layers making each other worse.
papers.kw: doctrine paper ai risk layers policy

papers.name: Three Roads From Here
papers.tech: The three positions on frontier AI (safety through development, acceleration, pause) characterized on their strongest terms, with existential and suffering risk treated as separate axes that do not always move together. The central frame: the camps are reading three different payoff matrices for the same game.
papers.plain: Three camps argue about powerful AI: keep building carefully, go faster, or pause. This paper explains all three fairly, shows there are two different worst cases rather than one, and plays the future out as a game to find the most likely outcome.
points: the race cannot be stopped, only won
a future that continues, and hurts
one matrix, three readings, edit the payoffs
papers.kw: doctrine paper ai safety acceleration pause game theory

papers.name: Two Stories About the Beginning
papers.tech: The Big Bang and a generated origin are the same kind of story: a starting condition plus a rule, with the evidence only ever reaching the rule. Four objections (tidiness, cheating, motive, proving too much) are taken seriously; two of them force the second story to change, and it survives as a testable rival rather than an evasion.
papers.plain: Physics says the universe started hot and dense and then the rules ran. A second story keeps the same start and the same rules and only changes who set them running. From inside you cannot tell the two apart, and this paper explains why that is not a problem with either story.
points: every origin story, and the evidence reaches only the rule
the first story already carries the extra layer
no shortcuts; the saving is that the rule is short
dropped; the process only has to exist and run
a rival commits to something, an evasion to nothing
finite grain, finite information, more room outside

guidance.title: AMA guidance
guidance.label: An outside standard, and this site's answers to it.
guidance.name: A Governance Framework for Agentic AI Assuming Clinical Functions
guidance.issuer: American Medical Association, Center for Digital Health and AI
guidance.tech: The AMA's framework sets out four questions for any AI that takes on clinical work, under one principle: **clinical authority is earned through evidence and maintained through demonstrated performance**. Nothing here is that kind of AI. The questions are still the right ones to ask of software built for medicine with AI, so each is answered below.
guidance.plain: The American Medical Association published four questions to ask of any AI doing medical work: what does it do, what proves it works, what is it allowed to do, and who answers for it. **Authority has to be earned with evidence.** None of these apps is a clinical AI, but the questions still apply, so here are the answers.
guidance.reviewed: The AMA has not reviewed or endorsed this site. The answers are the author's.
guidance.rights: Figure © 2026 American Medical Association. All rights reserved. Shown for reference, with a link to the source.

figure.alt: The AMA's governance framework for agentic AI in clinical functions: four steps (function, evidence and risk, authority and oversight, accountability), the governing principle that clinical authority is earned through evidence and maintained through demonstrated performance, and a continuous flywheel of deploy, monitor, learn and reassess.

points: What clinical function is the AI performing?
None. The medical works teach and help people study. None documents, triages, diagnoses or prescribes for a patient, and each one says so.
What shows it can perform, and what happens if it fails?
Claims are checked against a source and against the live app, and medical facts carry their citations. Where a review did not run, the page says so rather than claim it.
What should it be permitted to do, and under what conditions?
Inform, never decide or act. The calculators carry a visible note that they are flagged for clinician review, and known clinical defects wait for a clinician before they change.
Who is responsible for the risks and outcomes?
The author, who specified every system. AI wrote most of the code and answers for none of it. Corrections are logged, and earlier editions are kept, not deleted.
This page asks every address to answer while you read, every description was checked again against its live app for this edition, and the next model class rebuilds the site from a blank page.

guidance.kw: ama governance framework agentic ai clinical authority accountability oversight evidence
guidance.note: This section tracks the AMA's guidance as it is issued. Each new publication gets an entry in the timeline, and the site is checked against it again, so it stays aligned with the AMA.

timeline.title: A Governance Framework for Agentic AI Assuming Clinical Functions
timeline.text: The framework governs AI that takes on clinical functions in practice: an agent that documents, triages, diagnoses or treats inside a patient's care. That is the frontier as it lands in practice, and it is a separate realm from the study tools found here, which teach and never act. The site was checked against the framework's four questions and its flywheel.
checks: Function
Every medical work states its use: teaching and exam preparation, not medical advice.
Function
No work documents, triages, diagnoses, treats or prescribes for a patient.
Evidence + risk
Medical facts carry their citations, and scoring tables cite the governing publication.
Evidence + risk
Every description was checked again against its live app on 9 November 2026.
Evidence + risk
Where a review did not run, the page says so rather than claim it.
Authority + oversight
The tools inform and never decide or act; the calculators say to verify against current references before clinical use.
Authority + oversight
Known clinical defects are held for a clinician's sign-off before they change.
Accountability
The author, who specified every system, answers for it; AI is the engineering tool.
Accountability

The flywheel
